name: SRD5A3-CDG (CDG-Iq)
aliases: congenital disorder of glycosylation type Iq

reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: A dolichol-synthesis CDG caused by deficiency of the polyprenol reductase encoded by SRD5A3, needed to generate dolichol for glycosylation
Characterised by prominent ophthalmological involvement, including optic nerve and retinal anomalies, coloboma, nystagmus and visual impairment
Neurological features include developmental delay, hypotonia, cerebellar signs and sometimes seizures
Ichthyosiform skin changes and variable dysmorphism may be present
As a defect upstream in dolichol production, it impairs lipid-linked oligosaccharide assembly and gives a type I transferrin pattern
Management is supportive, with early ophthalmological and developmental input; no specific corrective therapy exists
Diagnosis is confirmed by SRD5A3 molecular genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: SRD5A3 encodes polyprenol reductase, which converts polyprenol to dolichol, the lipid carrier required to build the oligosaccharide precursor for N-glycosylation and other glycan pathways. Reduced dolichol availability limits assembly of the lipid-linked oligosaccharide, so N-linked sites are under-occupied and transferrin shows a type I pattern. The strikingly ocular-predominant phenotype reflects the sensitivity of eye development to glycosylation, while widespread hypoglycosylation accounts for the neurological, cutaneous and dysmorphic features.
additionalDifferentials: Other dolichol-pathway and type I CDG subtypes (e.g. DOLK-CDG, DPM1-CDG)
Isolated congenital ocular malformation syndromes (coloboma, optic nerve hypoplasia)
Peroxisomal and mitochondrial disorders with visual involvement
Other causes of infantile visual impairment with developmental delay
additionalInvestigations: Transferrin isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry showing a type I pattern
Detailed ophthalmological assessment including retinal and optic nerve evaluation
Neuroimaging for cerebellar and structural anomalies
redFlags: Progressive visual loss or severe congenital ocular malformation
Developmental regression or worsening cerebellar signs
Failure to thrive with multisystem involvement
reference.prognosis: Visual impairment is often significant and may progress, while neurodevelopmental outcome varies with disease severity; overall prognosis depends on the burden of neurological and systemic complications. There is no treatment that corrects the underlying defect.
pitfalls: Managing the eye findings in isolation without recognising an underlying glycosylation disorder
Misattributing the transferrin abnormality to secondary causes
Delaying molecular testing when a type I pattern accompanies ocular anomalies
references: Scriver's OMMBID, dolichol pathway disorders of glycosylation
Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics, disorders of glycosylation
management: No therapy corrects the underlying dolichol-synthesis defect; management is supportive and multidisciplinary
Early and ongoing ophthalmological care for optic nerve and retinal anomalies, coloboma and nystagmus, with correction of refractive error and low-vision support
Developmental support with physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy, and management of hypotonia
Antiseizure medication where seizures occur, alongside management of cerebellar signs
Emollient skin care for the ichthyosiform changes
Monitor coagulation and liver function given the risk of glycosylation-related coagulopathy and hepatic involvement
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder, with family screening and reproductive options
